I have always loved the holiday season.
People gathering and enjoying the
beautiful chaos of food and festivities
and families, visiting the winter
wonderland of Wakefield Court, and the
Grace Baptist Church Orchestra and Choir
who reintroduce us to the spirit and
meaning of Christmas with sacred hymns
and glorious fanfare at their annual
Christmas concert. This past Christmas
day, instead of sitting with my brothers
and reliving stories of our youth that
had far less aches and pains and far
more impressive hairlines, I would find
myself alone. Driving from Cape
Canaveral back home to Los Angeles, a
true coast to coast trip. I learned a
few things along the way. Gas really is
a lot cheaper in any other state instead
of California. The sun sets on the Texas
plains, as TL in the TV series Land Man
claims, really are special. and 40 plus
hours of staring at a windshield really
does provide a few moments for
reflection and introspection.
With each year's end, people of
different faith and traditions all find
time to give thanks. Thanksgiving
originating from the harvest festival
where we give thanks for the blessings
of the food from a successful harvest.
Diwali, the Hindu festival that
celebrates the triumph of good over evil
and a time that we give thanks for
prosperity, family, and abundance.
Quanza, the African-American cultural
holiday that focuses on gratitude,
reflection, and community through a
candle lighting on the canara and a
communal feast. And of course, Hanukkah,
an 8-day Jewish celebration
commemorating the lighting of the
manora, being a sign of God's ongoing
protection and emphasizes gratitude for
freedom, for miracles, and blessings.
Culturally, we all have traditions that
show gratitude to what this gift of life
has provided each and every one of us.
But why do we let those moments slip
away? When the lights come down and our
sacred times of reflections come to an
end, our appreciation often dims as
well. But it's predictable. Hydonic
adaptation is the human tendency for
returning to a relatively stable
baseline of happiness, which leads to
more cycles of seeking purpose, of
seeking new happiness. We are wired to
forget our gratefulness and continually
seek to find it again. The daily grind
of paying bills, going to work, getting
outraged or inspired over the news of
the day, all of it motivates us to
strive and to push for that next moment
of happiness, that next moment of
victory, and that next moment of
purpose. Tonight, I would ask us all to
simply pause for just a moment. Instead
of always rushing to yell, opine, and
convince yourself and others that
everything you're dealing with in the
world is worse than it's ever been, take
TL's advice. He says, "Sometimes the
best thing a person can do is just be
silent and enjoy things while you can.
There is always a desire to seek new
levels of fulfillment, just as there is
always time to embrace the gifts we have
now, but perhaps have temporarily
forgotten. I hope you all had a peaceful
and reflectful holiday season, and that
2026 is a year of hope, of fulfillment,
and of blessings yet realized. Thank
you, Mayor.

construction workers will visit their
